item.title: Breaking into cloud in 2026: A case study for new engineers
item.description:
Getting into IT from scratch is harder than it used to be, and the Australian market is in a rather strange spot right now. The path I took to get into the industry was once a completely plausible one. It’s still technically possible to follow, but it’s far less common today, and AI certainly isn’t making it any easier.

My own start was a little unconventional on paper. I left school at 15, did hospitality for 3 years, took a break, and then started my IT career at 22 on a helpdesk. Along the way I chased vendor certifications, passing some and failing others. They had little bearing on getting my foot in the door, as the technologies I trained on weren’t ones I used immediately. I remained at level 1 for 5 years, taking phone calls and doing basic tasks. However, during that time, I was also focused on career progression. For me, that came in the form of studying, networking (with people, not routers and switches), asking questions and forming relationships. Eventually I moved into infrastructure engineering, which has since evolved into platform engineering or DevOps engineering depending on how you look at it. In a previous blog I talked about how I was “conditioned” like others to grow this way.

item.title: The "Everything" engineer: Why industry expectations are getting out of hand
item.description:
I’m a frequent user of Reddit. I find it fascinating some of the stories that I read, from AusCorp, where someone is complaining about having to do a white collar role for the next 40 years and being miserable.
